New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

items.title: We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from ba
items.content:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8

New on our Science Blog: How AI is beginning to change scientific modeling.

Scientific models help researchers explain and predict real-world systems—like how a single nerve cell fires, or what happens when neutron stars collide. Recent advances have transformed how scientists fit complex models to data. But scientists still typically write the models manually, and usually need to weigh up several competing versions, each of which might explain the data in a different way.

In a guest post, Jakob Macke, Daniel Gedon, and Stefan Wahl describe how AI is starting to help with these parts of the process. By writing, running, fitting, and revising scientific models as code, AI can explore many possible model structures, and find out which explanations the data support.

So the crackle, the pops, the wow/flutter, the dull inner grooves are natural byproducts of the simulation. You can also "DJ" the record.

items.content:
There are a few notable counter-examples (e.g. HAL) but this is basically right for a lot of pre-2000 sci-fi.

I think getting AI right from e.g. somewhere in the ~1970s would require a fairly complicated set of inferences, probably the biggest things would be:

Image the world in 50 years.
1. "Digital knowledge work / computing". The vast majority of knowledge work (which makes up a very large fraction of the economy) goes digital. As computers get cheaper, much of society’s work happens on screens, over billions of machines in homes and offices.
2. "Internet". Similar to ARPANET (and see Licklider’s “Intergalactic Computer Network” (1963)), this creates demand for a global network of computers where people work, argue, teach, joke, and socialize.
3. "Big data". This creates a very large, compounding repository of digital information, with traces of how people reason, how they create, what they know etc.
4. "Statistical learning". Trying to program intelligence by hand is extremely difficult. But Shannon's n-gram approximations of English (1948) show examples of how language has statistical structure that can be "learned". You could imagine doing so over extensions of cybernetic computing (e.g. in the style of Rosenblatt's Perceptron 1958). So instead of programming thought, we could fit a statistical model to the record.
5. "LLMs". This might lead to something along the lines of ELIZA (1966), but with enough data (per 1-3), and enough compute (see Moore's law 1965), the imitation might become of extreme hight fidelity to the point that it's economically extremely useful.
6. "Scaling laws". These networks may demand a huge amount of data / computing resources and expertise to train. It's plausible that the more of each you have, the better your ELIZA gets. The economics concentrate, where a few organizations build a few minds and then deploy copies of them digitally.

Something like that. Basically, it's a lot of leaps. You have to start with computers, to internet, to big data, to big compute (Moore's law), which then allow large-scale statistical learning approach based on neural networks, and then posit scaling laws, and then imagine the form factor of language models as a lot more sophisticated ELIZA. And you'd have to short everything else, most predominantly I think the idea that we'd figure out how to program robots by hand.

very crazy to think about the degree of sheer brilliance of this group when we were just teenagers, and so special to see so many go on to leave their mark on the world.

items.title:
The P in JEPA stands for predictive.
The main distinction is not between JEA and JEPA, but between Joint Embedding (pred
items.content:
The P in JEPA stands for predictive.
The main distinction is not between JEA and JEPA, but between Joint Embedding (predictive or not) and generative architectures.
Whether a predictor is necessary depends on the task.

Given observations x and y (y being available only during training), a generative architectures predicts y from x. The loss is the divergence between y and its prediction:
  L = divergence(y, pred(enc(x)) )

A JEA encodes y as well and minimizes the divergence between the representations of x and y, while preventing collapse:
  L = divergence( enc(y), enc(x) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )
Where R is the anti-collapse regularizer, which may be computed over a batch of samples.
JEA are used when the prediction has no particular direction, i.e. when x and y are different views of the same scene. The idea for JEA is very old. Becker and Hinton proposed a simple model in 1989 where the anticollapse was based on information maximization. Schmidhuber had a version in 1992 based on redundancy minimization. At NIPS 1993, I proposed Siamese nets, which was a contrastive method to train JEA. Such contrastive methods gained popu.arity after Google's SimCLR paper in 2020. In 2021, Stéphane Deny in my group proposed the Barlow Twins redundancy reduction regularizer, which seemed to work at scale. This was shortly followed by VICReg by Adrien Bardes, Jean Ponce, and me, and last year by SIGReg by Randall Balestriero and me. 
DINO is a JEA method that comes from a long string of papers from Piotr Bojanowski's group at FAIR-Paris, starting with Noise as Targets (2017), Deep Clustering (2018-2020), and DINO v1-v3 which are contrastive between clusters, not samples.

JEPA adds a predictor, which is useful when the prediction is non-symetric. For example, when x is a degraded/corrupted version of y, or when x is a present observation and y a future observation (temporal prediction). The loss is:
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x)) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

All of these models can be augmented by an action variable a, fed to the predictor, encoding an action, intervention, or transformation to produce y from x.
This turns the system into a "world model". In a JEPA, the loss becomes
  L = divergence( enc(y), pred(enc(x), a) ) + R( enc(y), enc(x) )

items.content:
AI can now help turn a published fix into a working exploit in hours. Patching still takes weeks, and for many old routers, cameras, and supermarket fridges, a fix never arrives.

"So the question isn't how to patch faster. It's how to stop needing to."

Six openings for new cybersecurity companies today, each one making patching "unnecessary, or someone else's job":

1. Live fixes: blocks an exploit on running systems within hours, then has AI write and ship the real code fix

2. An AI first responder: spots attacks without hand-written rules and contains them as they unfold

3. Per-request access: checks every request from a person or their AI agents, with credentials that expire in minutes

4. Proven recovery: keeps restoring your backups in a sealed-off test environment to prove they work, with records insurers will accept

5. An install gateway: holds and sandboxes every package, extension and AI agent tool before it can run

6. Security for the long tail: one managed service for water utilities, clinics and others that will never have a security team

items.content:
now that apple put xcode inside claude code, here’s how i’d find, build and grow an iOS app with AI agents:

find it
- open appfigures or sensor tower and sort utilities by revenue
- filter for apps with a rating under 3.5
- bonus points if the top app hasn't shipped an update in 6+ months
- check the keywords they rank for in appfigures. low difficulty + high revenue is the sweet spot
- scroll the "you might also like" row on the top app's page. every app there is another market to check
- or find a startup idea on https://t.co/a5ARFnvky2 based on social sentiment

validate it
- use facundoolano/app-store-scraper to pull every review for the top 20
- give them to an agent: "cluster the 1 and 2 star reviews into the top 5 complaints and quote the users"
- pick the app where the complaints are about the product, not the price
- if people complain about the price but keep paying, that's demand. if they complain about bugs, that's your opening
- search reddit for "alternative to [app]". every thread is a list of people waiting for you

build it
- claude code + apple's new xcode plugin to build, preview and fix
- cameroncooke/XcodeBuildMCP so the agent can build, test and run the simulator on its own
- joshuayoes/ios-simulator-mcp so it can tap, swipe and screenshot like a user
- write a skill with the top 5 complaints so every feature gets checked against them
- apple's foundation models for on-device ai, so your inference cost is $0
- app intents so siri and personal agents can use your app too
- add an "import from [competitor]" button. make switching take 10 seconds

test it
- maestro tests every flow the reviewers complained about
- the agent runs them on every screen size before each build
- if the competitor's worst flow takes 6 taps, yours takes 2
- sentry for crashes, telemetrydeck for analytics
- testflight it to 20 people from those reddit threads before launch

monetize it
- revenuecat for subscriptions and mrr
- superwall to test paywalls without shipping a new build
- paywall right after the first win, never on launch
- annual as the default with a 3-day trial, weekly as the anchor
- turn on win-back offers for everyone who cancels

rank it
- your screenshots answer each complaint directly. "no ads." "works offline." "cancel anytime."
- fastlane snapshot + frameit regenerates every screenshot automatically
- a/b test them with app store connect's product page optimization
- have the agent localize your listing into 10 languages. most competitors only rank in english
- ask for a review right after a win with apple's built-in review prompt, never after an error

grow it
- find 10 creators in your niche on tiktok one. small monthly base + a bonus for every 100k views
- give each one a fresh tiktok account that only posts about your niche
- apify's tiktok scraper pulls the top 100 hooks in your niche every week. that's your hook bank
- every creator tests 3 new hooks a day in capcut. anything that loses people in the first 3 seconds gets cut
- arcads or heygen for ai ugc when you need 50 variations of a winner
- postiz to schedule everything across tiktok, reels and shorts
- faceless slideshow accounts posting 3x a day: problem, screenshot, result
- when an organic video takes off, put money behind it with tiktok spark ads instead of making new ads
- a unique apple offer code for every creator so you know exactly who drove each subscriber
- a quiz landing page on framer that ends in "download the app." web-to-app funnels convert better than cold traffic
- appsflyer to track which video, creator and ad actually turned into revenue
- apple ads on the competitor's name

i could do a whole episode on @startupideaspod if people are interested. i will never gatekeep anything im learning in real-time.

welcome to the golden age of ios apps, because now anyone can build one

Nobody has ever explained all of Claude to you.

But here's everything about Claude you must know:

Level 1. Don't be la
items.content:
Nobody has ever explained all of Claude to you.

But here's everything about Claude you must know:

Level 1. Don't be lazy, use the Claude desktop app.

You will still use the browser 90% of the time, and that's fine. But the day you start using the Claude desktop app, you'd be able to work with your folders without ever uploading the files one by one. You'd use Claude code more. There is no coming back from there.

Level 2. You have better things to do than spending 1 minute choosing the best model.

Default should be: Opus 5.5 on high. That's it.

Do not switch the models mid-chat. It consumes more tokens because Claude re-reads the entire chat (again) to get the context.

Level 3. Either Medium or High effort. Nothing else

Medium when it is low-effort work. High for most of the tasks. But Extra High mostly burn through your usage limit.

Level 4. Delete your old Claude setup.

Delete the “Instructions for Claude” box in settings. Delete the old added Claude skills. Old skills and prompts might be slowing you down since they were written for old models. Instead, give one goal and end prompts with: “Before you start, restate my goal in your own words.”

Level 5. Ask for HTML. Not for a document.

Add two things to your prompt: “Make it an HTML page” and “for [who will read it].”

Claude will code the image, doc, or any other format. There is no scope of making mistakes.

Level 6. Protect what you plug in.

Never click the thumbs up or down under an answer. You are basically giving feedback to AI, and they are allowed to send it to their training data. On a Team plan, once memory is on, leave it on: if an owner turns it off, every member’s memories are deleted permanently.

Your first 20 minutes, in order:

1. Install desktop app.
2. No settings are the best.
3. Connect ONE tool - not everything.
4. Use Claude Code more than you do.
5. Delete the installed skills, and add the new ones (written for the latest models)
6. Go to https://t.co/cn6xDN1uAS for my Claude skill library.

I can't believe my Claude saved me $10,200/year (without accessing my bank account or money) with this copy-paste prompt:

But before blindly doing it.

→ Start by reading this: https://t.co/38nzKYzEFG.

→ Go to all your bank accounts apps.
→ Download 12 months of transactions as CSV files.
→ Put the CSV files in a folder on your desktop.
→ Go to Claude. Set it to Opus 5.5 on 'High.'
→ Open the CSV files folder in Claude.
→ Paste this prompt (with your context):

"Be my CFO.

Goal: find every place I lose money, and tell me exactly what to cut, keep, switch or renegotiate, biggest money first.

Context: I attached the transaction exports (CSV) of every bank account and card I use. Each bank uses a different format, currency and date range. Some accounts may be for my business.

Work in 5 steps. Use code for every number: never estimate a total by reading.

STEP 1. Clean

Read every file. For each one, tell me: bank, account, currency, first and last date, number of transactions.

Put everything in one table: date, account, merchant (cleaned: “SQ *JOES COFFEE 4421” becomes “Joe’s Coffee”), amount, currency.

Find the money that only moves between my own accounts: transfers, savings, paying my card bill, currency conversions, refunds. Take it out of spending, so nothing counts twice. If I pay a card you don’t have the file for, tell me.

Group charges billed through Apple, Google, PayPal, Amazon or any other middleman by amount and day of the month, so each hidden subscription shows on its own line.

STEP 2. First look

Show me, for the whole period and per month: money in, money out, what’s left. Then my cost centers (housing, food, transport, software, subscriptions, insurance, fees, travel, business…) from biggest to smallest, and every recurring charge (weekly, monthly, yearly) with its price and when it renews next.

STEP 3. Ask me

Stop here and ask me 5 to 10 questions, with clickable options when you can. Only ask what changes your advice: where I live, my job, who I pay for, which accounts are business, what I’m saving for, and what each charge you can’t name is. Wait for my answers.

STEP 4. The audit, cost center by cost center, biggest first

For each cost center:

- What I spend per month and per year, and whether it’s going up.
- What’s normal for someone like me (my job, my country, my household), and how you know.
- Every merchant inside it, scored: KEEP, WATCH or CUT, with one line why.
- What I’d save per year if I act.

Then hunt for:

> Ghost subscriptions: things I pay for and probably forgot. Ask me if you’re not sure.
> Odd charges: the same charge twice, a price that went up, a free trial that turned paid, a charge after I cancelled, tiny test charges, merchants you can’t identify.
> Fees: bank, card, ATM, currency conversion, late fees, interest.
> Business, if I have...."

PS: I couldn't paste the entire prompt here.

A TermiX Skill can act for your account. What did you actually authorize?

@termix_ai  public toolkit instructs users to
items.content:
A TermiX Skill can act for your account. What did you actually authorize?

@termix_ai  public toolkit instructs users to install the Skill package, then approve a webpage link so the Agent can act as the user’s account. Each chain is linked separately. The statement establishes account-level access. It does not define the scope, spending allowance, expiry, or per-transaction signing policy of that link.

Four distinct steps are often treated as one action.

Installing the skill loads executable workflow logic into the agent runtime. This step precedes account linking and is analytically separate from it. Linking the terminal creates the “acts as your account” standing on the chosen chain. The public materials confirm the link exists and is chain-specific. They do not describe its permission surface, lifetime, or revocation path.

Authenticating API calls is documented more clearly. Public read endpoints, API keys, EIP-191 wallet-message signatures, and on-chain wallet signatures are treated as different functions. Examples in the authentication documentation are associated with the BSC Testnet environment. API authentication does not by itself authorize fund movement.

Signing the transaction is handled in the TypeScript SDK through two modes. Mode A returns an unsigned EVM transaction intent and requires no injected Signer. Mode B injects an application-controlled Signer so the SDK can sign, broadcast, and wait for finality. Mode A leaves the final signature outside the SDK’s injected path; an external system can still automate that signature. Mode B places the signing decision inside the application that holds the key. The browser-approved terminal-link flow has not been shown to use exactly the same mechanism as either mode.

Account linking lets the Agent operate under the user’s identity for commercial actions. It does not transfer private-key custody. The user or the application that controls the signing key decides whether a transaction is submitted. Automated commerce can generate sequences of orders, escrow deposits, and settlements. Each step still depends on who holds the key and what limits, if any, constrain the linked session.

The natural unit of agent commerce is the individual job: a request, a quote, an escrow deposit, a delivery, and a settlement. An account-level standing is broader than a single job. Whether the production link is scoped to specific actions or inherits wider account capabilities is not specified in the current public onboarding materials.

Developers can verify network selection, the exact permissions approved during the webpage link, and the resulting transaction records. Spending limits, session expiry, and revocation mechanics are not fully described in those materials. Evidence that an Agent completed a paid job without broader authority would include the transaction hashes, the linked session parameters, and confirmation that no additional approvals were granted beyond the commercial actions.

The promotional post that encourages installing Skills supplies context. It does not establish new spending limits or independently tested security guarantees. The documented layers define a boundary. The precise production enforcement of account-link scope, expiry, and revocation remains subject to further verification.

“My worry is that it will be broad, and it will be faster than what we’ve seen with previous technology.”

In 42 seconds, he named the people exposed first:

→ entry-level consultants
→ junior lawyers
→ financial professionals
He also gave a number:
50% of entry-level white-collar jobs could disappear - pushing unemployment to 10–20% within 1–5 years.

This isn’t another factory automation cycle.

Previous technology replaced one narrow task at a time.

AI can research, summarize, analyze documents, write code and communicate across the same knowledge job.

junior does the work → senior reviews it → junior becomes senior

New model:

items.content:
🧊 An AI agent can now build a complete 3D washing machine with moving parts in just 38 lines of code. No complicated Blender scripting required.

Sandflow has released sand3d, an open-source Python library designed specifically for LLMs and AI coding agents.

Instead of forcing an AI to write hundreds of lines of Blender Python, sand3d provides a compact modeling vocabulary for creating geometry, assembling objects, and defining mechanical movement.

And the results are actual 3D assets, not just rendered images.

🔧 What can sand3d create?

▪️ 3D geometry with precise dimensions, profiles, holes, and curved surfaces.

▪️ Complex assemblies made from individually named components.

▪️ Mechanical joints, hinges, sliders, and rotating parts.

▪️ Parametric objects that can be modified by changing a few values.

▪️ Exportable models for games, CAD workflows, and robotics simulators.

🧺 A complete washing machine in 38 lines

The developers demonstrate a washing machine with:

▪️ A cabinet and internal rotating drum.

▪️ A hinged door with glass and handle.

▪️ A sliding detergent drawer.

▪️ A rotating control dial.

The assembly includes four defined joints, so its components can move independently.

You can inspect the object in an interactive viewer and manipulate individual joints.

⚡ Up to 6× fewer tokens

Sandflow compared its code against other procedural modeling systems.

Median token-count ratios:

▪️ Blender Python: 4.0× as many tokens.

▪️ CadQuery: 2.3×.

▪️ FeatureScript: 6.0×.

▪️ Articraft SDK: 2.0×.

These are developer-reported comparisons on selected CAD and articulated objects, not a universal measure of model-generation performance.

🧠 The entire API fits into approximately 3,600 tokens.

That's one of the most interesting details.

An AI agent can receive the complete API reference in its context, then use a relatively small vocabulary to construct objects programmatically.

Parts, faces, and edges are referenced by name rather than manually calculating every coordinate.

The process is deterministic: running the same program produces the same mesh.

📦 Export to real 3D workflows

▪️ GLB: Meshes, materials, and joint metadata for viewers and game engines.

▪️ URDF: Articulated structures with joint limits for MuJoCo, Isaac, ROS, and other robotics tools.

▪️ USD: Structured scenes for OpenUSD workflows.

▪️ OBJ / STL: Static geometry for conventional 3D tools and fabrication.

🚀 Open source and ready to install

pip install sand3d

The library runs on Blender's bpy engine and supports Python 3.11 and 3.13. Python 3.12 is currently unsupported.

Sandflow also provides a collection of approximately 100,000 programmatically described 3D assets, with datasets available on Hugging Face.

Everything is released under Apache 2.0.

One important distinction: sand3d isn't a generative AI model itself. It's a modeling toolkit that lets language models produce executable 3D programs.

And that's potentially even more useful for certain workflows.

Instead of generating a mesh that's difficult to modify, an agent can create structured, editable geometry with explicit components and mechanical relationships.

A promising direction for AI-assisted CAD, game assets, robotics, and procedural 3D production.
